analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from forcing workers to arbitrate job disputes instead of going to court.
analysis.headline: The bill to end forced arbitration at work never left the Senate committee it was referred to; no hearing, vote, or floor action was ever taken before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Most large employers today require workers, as a condition of getting the job, to sign away their right to sue in court and to join class actions; disputes go to private arbitration instead. This bill would make those mandatory agreements unenforceable. Workers could still choose arbitration after a dispute arises, but only freely, with a 45-day waiting period and written notice. It would also change the National Labor Relations Act so employers cannot punish workers for refusing to give up those rights.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers — including independent contractors regardless of how they are labeled — who would regain the right to take wage theft, discrimination, and other job disputes to court and to band together in class or collective actions, which is often the only way a single worker can afford to bring a claim. The bill's own findings say forced individual arbitration leads to widespread nonenforcement of workers' rights and that many workers seek no redress at all for fear of retaliation.

how_it_helps.text: Makes any pre-dispute arbitration agreement covering a work dispute invalid and unenforceable, and voids any pre-dispute waiver of the right to join a joint, class, or collective action.

Allows arbitration only after a dispute arises, and only if it is genuinely voluntary: not required by the employer, not a condition of employment, disclosed in plain language, agreed to in writing, and signed after a 45-day waiting period during which the clock on the worker's claims is paused.
Covers independent contractors no matter what label the company uses, and extends to domestic workers in households.

Adds an unfair labor practice making it illegal for an employer to force, coerce, or retaliate against a worker for refusing to promise not to join a group claim, and gives workers a private right to sue over retaliation with attorney's fees.

The bill's findings state that most workers have little or no meaningful choice about arbitration clauses and often do not know they have given up their day in court, and that joining a class action is often the only affordable way to seek relief.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that use mandatory arbitration clauses — especially large companies and gig-economy platforms — would lose a private, cheaper, class-action-free channel for resolving disputes and would face more lawsuits and class actions over wages, discrimination, and working conditions. Arbitration providers would lose a large block of business. Some disputes might take longer and cost more to resolve through court litigation.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not ban arbitration entirely — it permits voluntary post-dispute arbitration with a 45-day waiting period and written consent — but it still shifts more disputes into court, where cases can take years and cost more for everyone involved than a single arbitration.

Employers have long argued that individual arbitration is faster and cheaper for workers with a single claim, and that class actions primarily benefit plaintiffs' lawyers; courts have repeatedly enforced arbitration clauses on that theory, and workers who prefer a quick individual resolution would lose that default option.

The bill carves out arbitration provisions in collective bargaining agreements negotiated with unions, meaning unionized workers remain governed by their contract's own dispute system rather than the new protections.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a worker with a wage-theft or discrimination claim worth a few thousand dollars, a class action is often the only economically possible route, and forced arbitration blocks it; that is the problem this bill exists to fix, and the tradeoff is more court litigation and higher costs for employers. The bill tries to blunt the objection by keeping voluntary, post-dispute arbitration available with real consent safeguards rather than banning the practice outright.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate labor committee, where it sat with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Patty Murray introduced the Restoring Justice for Workers Act on June 11, 2024, with 18 fellow Democratic and independent senators listed as original cosponsors.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

The full action history shows nothing after that referral: the HELP Committee never held a markup or vote on the bill, and the Senate never took it up before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

The bill's findings trace the problem to Supreme Court decisions, including Epic Systems Corp. v. Lewis (2018), which held that employers may require workers to waive the right to act collectively as a condition of employment.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that require workers to sign forced arbitration and class-action waivers keep that system in place: workplace disputes stay in individual, private arbitration and large group claims remain blocked, so violations can continue without court scrutiny.

for.name: Patty Murray
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 18 Democratic and independent cosponsors.

for.name: 17 of 48 Senate Democrats and 2 of 4 Senate independents
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors of the bill at introduction.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 11, 2024 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote at any point in the Congress.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and large employer groups
against.what_they_did: Have consistently lobbied against federal bans on forced arbitration in employment, which they say keeps dispute resolution faster and cheaper than court litigation.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or independents (17 of 48 Senate Democrats and 2 of 4 independents); no Republican signed on, and no vote was ever held to test broader support.

industries.industry: Large employers and gig-economy platforms that use mandatory arbitration
industries.note: These companies would lose the ability to channel workplace disputes into private, individual arbitration and block class actions, exposing them to more lawsuits over wages, discrimination, and conditions. The bill's findings say the current system has produced widespread nonenforcement of workers' rights.

Mandatory employment arbitration is a major line of paid business for private arbitration firms; the ban on pre-dispute agreements removes that revenue stream, though voluntary post-dispute arbitration remains available.

industries.industry: Plaintiffs' employment and class-action law firms
industries.note: With arbitration clauses unenforceable, workers can again bring court claims and class actions, and the bill provides attorney's fees for retaliation suits — expanding work for lawyers who represent workers. Some critics note class litigation also enriches plaintiffs' attorneys.
